1:
The psalm opens without a title, and the witnesses first take account of that silence and of the abrupt cry it frames — "why standest thou afar off, O LORD? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble?" The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make the opening a question of the psalm's very identity: this and Psalm 33 are the only anonymous psalms in the First book, and the Septuagint joins this one to Psalm 9 as a single song, not without warrant, for both are laid out in tetrastichs and this one begins with the letter lamed, taking up the alphabet where the ninth psalm left it. The six strophes that follow drop the letters from mem to tsade, and only at the close do the last four resume the acrostic — so that the two psalms together compose one broken alphabet, and the reader who feels the abruptness of the opening is feeling the seam.

The latin-fathers Augustine hears in the very delay a design of mercy: God despises "in due seasons, in tribulations," that is, seasonably, causing tribulations to inflame men's minds with longing for his coming, for that fountain of life is the sweeter to them that have much thirst. The reformed voices, for their part, refuse to let the "afar off" be taken of place. John Gill grants that God by his infinite essence is everywhere and never far from any creature, so that the complaint speaks only of his withdrawing his gracious presence and deferring help; and John Calvin insists the words are spoken by anthropathy, attributing to God the passions and manner of men, for nothing can be hid from his eyes, and if he seems to take no notice it is the same, to our sense, as if he had withdrawn himself. Calvin reads the whole psalm as a mirror of a corrupt and disorganised society, held up that the faithful, seeing iniquity break out like a flood, may not fall into despair.

The puritan-evangelical witnesses turn the complaint inward. Matthew Henry owns that God's withdrawings are grievous to his people, especially in trouble, yet lays some of the fault at our own door: "we stand afar off from God by our unbelief, and then we complain that God stands afar off from us." Charles Spurgeon feels the wound of it keenly — it is not the trouble but the hiding of the Father's face that cuts to the quick — and steadies himself on the thought of the refiner who is never far from the mouth of the furnace when his gold is in the fire, remembering that there is a "needs-be" not only for trial but for heaviness of heart under it (1 Pet. 1:6). The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds only the historical setting, referring the psalm to the days of the captivity and the enemies who then beheld the oppression of God's people and seemed to disregard it.
2:
From the distant God the psalm turns to the near oppressor, and the witnesses fasten on the pairing of vice and violence in "the wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry divides the charge into its two counts, pride and persecution, the former the cause of the latter: proud men will have all about them to be of their mind, and those who will not yield to them they hate with an inveterate hatred, so that tyranny in state and church alike owes its origin to pride. Charles Spurgeon reads the verse as a formal indictment followed by the sufferer's petition, "let them be taken in the devices that they have imagined," and finds the prayer only just — "we weigh you in your own scales, and measure your corn with your own bushel" — the day of every persecuting Babylon, when Haman shall hang on his own gallows and the enemies of Daniel be cast into their own den of lions.

The reformed John Gill fixes the "poor" as the good and gracious man, commonly poor in the world's goods and poor in spirit, and reads the verb as one of hot pursuit, the persecutor following hard after his prey as antichrist has hunted the followers of the Lamb. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke can find no natural principle to account for such hatred: a wicked man persecutes a humble follower of God for his religion only because "the devil hates godliness, and the wicked man hates it also because the devil is in his heart."

But the grammatical-historical witnesses open a real question of the Hebrew. Charles Ellicott, following the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus, and the Vulgate, would make the sufferer, not the persecutor, the subject of the opening line: "in the pride of the wicked the sufferer burns," taken not of any indignation felt by the afflicted but literally of the affliction they endure. He carries the change into the second clause, where the plural quietly displaces the singular, "they, the sufferers, are taken in the plot which they, the wicked, have devised," the snare recoiling on its makers. Keil and Delitzsch keep the persecutor in view and mark how the perfect tenses record a settled character; the wicked man does not hide his shameful desire but makes it the very matter of loud self-praise, and is himself the covetous, rapacious man whom the next verse will name.

So the witnesses divide over the grammar without dividing over the sense. Whether the line says that the wicked in his pride hunts the poor, or that in the pride of the wicked the poor man burns, the pride and the persecution still stand together; and the prayer that the plotters be caught in their own plot is, all agree, the reasonable cry of the oppressed.
3:
The evidence on the count of pride is heard first, and the witnesses call the persecutor's own mouth to testify, for "the wicked boasteth of his heart's desire." The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon hears a boaster thrice condemned: a silly boaster, for he glories in a mere desire; a brazen-faced one, for that desire is villainy; and an abandoned sinner, to boast of what is his shame. The wesleyan-arminian voices agree that the vaunt is self-betraying. Adam Clarke has him boast among his fellows how often he has gratified his passions, and warns that "he who can boast of his iniquity is in the broad road to perdition"; John Wesley marks that he glories "in his very sins, which are his shame, and especially in the satisfaction of his desires."

The reformed John Gill reads the same self-applause, rendering the clause with the Chaldee and Jarchi, "the wicked praiseth himself for the desire of his heart," and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the boast against heaven's verdict: the sinner "blesses the covetous, whom the Lord abhors," so that God and men are seen to differ utterly in their sentiments of persons, since the friendship of the world is enmity with God.

Over the second half of the verse the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott opens a double difficulty of the Hebrew. He first renders the opening literally, "the wicked speaketh praise to the lust of his soul," and delights in the poetry of a villain addressing his own evil passions in laudatory terms, as the rich fool in the parable congratulated his soul. Then he presses that "blesseth" is "rather curseth, by a common euphemism," the same softened word used of Naboth's accusers and of Job's fear for his sons (Job 1:5); and since the word for "the covetous" — properly the robber — may stand as subject or object, the line may be read "the robber curseth and despiseth Jehovah," or "he greedily curseth, despiseth Jehovah," which he thinks the better echo of the first clause. The Septuagint and Vulgate, he notes, read differently again, "the sinner hath irritated the Lord."

Here the witnesses genuinely part. The received reading, kept by Gill and Henry, has the proud man bless and approve the covetous whom God abhors; Ellicott, with the ancient euphemism, has him curse and despise the LORD himself. Yet under either rendering the verse serves the same end, exhibiting a heart so at ease in its wickedness that it can turn even its greed into an object of praise, and make its own lust the god that it worships.
4:
The atheism latent in such pride now comes to the surface, and the witnesses read in the persecutor's very face his refusal of God — "the wicked, through the pride of his countenance, will not seek after God." The reformed John Gill supplies the object with the Targum and Kimchi, "after God," and takes the seeking for prayer and inquiry alike: the wicked will not seek to God for counsel nor cry to him for help, nor inquire into his will, but does what is right in his own eyes, and all of this springs from a pride of heart that shows itself in the haughty look, the countenance "more stout than his fellows." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears a man too proud to bend his knee before his Judge, too haughty to put on sackcloth and lie in the dust, and therefore, without deep repentance, certain to perish; and John Wesley notes that pride, though properly seated in the heart, is here named of the countenance because there it is most manifest.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a definition of irreligion itself: it is "not seeking after God, and not having him in our thoughts," a secret wish to have no dependence upon him and not to be beholden to him (Job 35:10); and its cause, again, is pride, for men will not seek after God because they think they have no need of him, their own hands being sufficient for them, and reckon it a thing below them to be religious.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott judges that the Authorised Version "has quite missed the meaning" of the verse, and would translate it altogether otherwise: "the wicked, in his haughtiness" — literally in the height of his nostril, the very gesture of turning up the nose at another — "saith, He will not requite it," that is, God will not punish; "there is no God in all his thought." On his reading the line does not merely say the wicked neglects to seek God, but puts into his mouth the settled creed of the fool, that there is no God who calls men to account, the same denial voiced in the fourteenth and fifty-third psalms (Ps. 14:1).

So a genuine difference of rendering runs beneath the verse: whether it describes the proud man's practical godlessness, his refusal to seek or think of God as Gill and Henry take it, or, with Ellicott, records the impious speech in which he denies that God will ever requite him. Either way the witnesses agree that the root is the same pride, and that a heart which will not look up has already, in effect, said there is no God above it.
5:
The wicked man's prosperity is the next scandal, and the witnesses labour over a line whose Hebrew has been read half a dozen ways — "his ways are always grievous." The reformed John Gill lays the renderings side by side: his ways "cause terror," as Aben Ezra has it, making men afraid; or are "defiled," with the Septuagint and Vulgate, since to him nothing is pure; or "always remain," never changing for the better; or, as Jarchi will have it, they "prosper," which is the very thing that stumbles the saints. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses toward the last of these, translating "his enterprises always succeed," or at least "his ways are always strong," the bold and reckless course with which a tyrant drives to his end. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads instead a labour of iniquity, "he is travailing in pain to bring forth iniquity at all times," full of unholy desire, conceiving and bringing forth sin until death itself is born.

Whatever the ways, the witnesses agree on what the man refuses to see. Gill, Clarke, and Ellicott all take "thy judgments are far above out of his sight" of a God whose reckonings are lifted so high above the sinner that they never trouble his conscience; Ellicott renders it literally "a height, thy judgments, far above him" (Ps. 36:6), and Clarke says the man is so blinded with sin that he cannot see the operations of God's hand. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears him turn off every warning: tell him of God's authority and he answers that he never saw God, tell him of God's judgments and he counts them mere bugbears, for they are far above out of his sight.

On the last clause the witnesses close ranks. "As for all his enemies, he puffeth at them" — Clarke has him whistle at them, insult God and despise men, overthrowing them with a breath, like the Eastern despot who needed only to say "bring me the head" and it was done; John Wesley makes the puffing a gesture of contempt, the man confident he can blow his foes away; and Ellicott, catching the same scorn, quotes South that "it is really to defy heaven to puff at damnation, and bid omnipotence do its work." The picture, on every reading, is of a man whose success has hardened into insolence — his ways prospering, or grievous, or strong, but his eye never once lifted to the judgments that hang, unseen and unfeared, above his head.
6:
Secure in that prosperity, the persecutor speaks the boast of a man who thinks himself beyond change: "I shall not be moved: for I shall never be in adversity." The reformed John Gill notes that this is said "in his heart," within himself, the thought being the word or speech of the mind, a settled inward persuasion rather than an open vaunt. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the ground of the confidence — "I have whatever I covet, I hold whatsoever I have gotten, I have money and goods to procure me every gratification" — the security of a man who mistakes abundance for permanence.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear something more dreadful in it, a blasphemous parody of faith. What the believer may truly say by reason of his fellowship with God, "I shall not be moved" (Ps. 16:8), the wicked says in godless self-confidence, looking upon himself in age after age, through the whole endless future, as one who will never be in evil case; and out of this boundless carnal security his mouth runs over with cursing. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, grants that the meaning is clear though the construction is involved, and offers as the best rendering, "I shall never be moved at any time: I who am without ill," the man congratulating himself as one whom evil can never touch.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the boast in the long line of doomed securities. The persecutor "sets trouble at defiance and is confident of the continuance of his own prosperity," pleasing himself with the thought that his goods are laid up for many years; he is like Babylon that said, "I shall be a lady for ever" (Isa. 47:7; Rev. 18:7). And Henry draws the sober moral that governs the verse: "those are nearest ruin who thus set it furthest from them," for the boast of an unmovable prosperity is itself the surest token that the fall is near.

The witnesses do not divide. Whether the words are read as the miser's contentment with his hoard, the atheist's parody of the saint's assurance, or the tyrant's dream of a perpetual reign, all hear in "I shall never be in adversity" the language of a presumption that has forgotten both the changeableness of earthly things and the God who alone stands unmoved; and all agree that such a heart, most sure of itself, is in truth the least secure.
7:
The catalogue of the persecutor's crimes now moves from his heart to his speech, and the witnesses hear a mouth that is a very arsenal — "his mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud." The reformed John Gill renders it "he has filled his mouth with cursing," and takes the word for an oath, whether the profane oath that takes God's name in vain or the false oath sworn to defraud, so that in the man of sin it becomes the mouth "speaking great things and blasphemies" against God and his saints. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the darker sense: from the joining of cursing with deceit, as in Hosea's "swearing and lying" (Hos. 4:2), we must understand perjury. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sums the portrait in a breath — "what a finished character! a blasphemer, a deceitful man, and a knave!" — while John Wesley draws out the hidden half of the verse, that under the fair and plausible speeches "mischief is hid and covered," the "vanity" of the last clause being better read as injury, the vexation and oppression of other men. The heaping of the terms — cursing, deceit, fraud, and, under the tongue, mischief and vanity — is itself a mark of the completeness of the corruption, a mouth that has left no room for a true or a kindly word.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the two faces of the tongue into one. The persecutors are bitter and malicious, and "where there is a heart full of malice there is commonly a mouth full of curses"; those they cannot really harm they will at least spit their venom at, breathing out the slaughter they cannot execute, so that God's faithful worshippers have been anathematised and cursed with bell, book, and candle. Yet the same mouth is false as well as fierce, its mischief hidden under the tongue, for the persecutor has learned of the devil to deceive and so to destroy, covering his hatred with deceit (Prov. 26:26).

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch begin here to draw the figure that will govern the next verses, the ungodly man as one lying in wait, and read the scene against a background of anarchy such as Hosea describes, where robber-bands lurk by the way (Hos. 6:9). The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the persecutor's speech is of a piece with his heart, cursing what it cannot reach and cloaking what it means to strike, a mouth full at once of open blasphemy and of covered fraud.
8:
The lurking that his speech concealed becomes, in this verse, a settled ambush, and the witnesses picture the persecutor as a highwayman of souls: "he sitteth in the lurking places of the villages." The reformed John Gill notes that the word may mean not the mean haunts of thieves but "palaces" or "courts," as the Chaldee and Syriac render it, and the Septuagint's "lurking places with the rich," so that the ambush is laid by persons of note — antichrist seated in the temple of God, his emissaries creeping into the congregations of the saints to corrupt their faith and manners. The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the plainer scene of the robber: Adam Clarke sees in it the setting of spies and the craft of the private murderer, who sits in secret places, his eyes privily set, lying in wait to catch the poor; John Wesley places him not within the villages but in the ways bordering them, as robbers use, watching from his lurking-place, the "privily set" of the verse being literally "hid."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott works at the two hard words. "Villages," he explains, is properly enclosed spaces, and so, like our word "town," comes to mean any collection of dwellings, even an unwalled place or a nomad's encampment (Gen. 25:16). Over "the poor" he lingers longest, for the Hebrew word here is peculiar to this psalm, recurring only in v.10 and v.14, and its root idea is darkness; whence, by an easy transition, it comes to mean the obscure and humble, though Ellicott records the suggestion of Mr. Burgess that the root sense be kept throughout, so that the line would run "his eyes hide," that is, wait, "for the darkness," the persecutor watching for the twilight as the adulterer does in Job (Job 24:15).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the ambush morally. Like Esau the cunning hunter the persecutor sits in the secret places with his eyes privily set, and not because he is ashamed, for if he blushed there were hope he would repent, nor because he fears God, whom he thinks will never call him to account, but only because he is afraid that the discovery of his design should defeat it. His malice is against the innocent, who never provoked him, and against the poor, over whom it will be no glory to triumph; and those are wholly lost to honour against whose plots neither innocence nor poverty is any security.
9:
"He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den" — the ambush of the last verse is now given the shape of a hunt, and the witnesses take up its double figure of lion and net. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the imagery with care. The lion's lair is named by a word that means a thicket, from a root signifying to interweave or cover over, with no connection to the word for a thorn; and they observe that in the second line the figure is reversed, for now the afflicted man is the prey and the wicked the hunter who drives him into the pit and drags him off in his net (Job 24:22). Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, frankly calls it "a confusion of metaphor," the wicked being first the lion watching for his prey and then the hunter snaring it, and renders the whole with a fine mounting repetition: "in his hiding-place he lurks, as a lion in his lair, lurks to seize a sufferer, seizes a sufferer, drawing him into his net."

The reformed John Gill reads the lion of antichrist in his twofold capacity, civil and ecclesiastical — the beast with the mouth of a lion and the voice of a dragon — and hears in the secret lying-in-wait the insidious methods by which the persecutor destroys the faithful witnesses of Christ, striking not in the open field but from cover.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry brings the two halves together in a single dreadful image: the persecutor "lies in wait as a lion that thirsts after blood, and feeds with pleasure upon the prey," and behind him stands the devil whose agent he is, that roaring lion who seeks "not what, but whom, he may devour." What the poor man suffers, on Henry's reading, is not a chance mishap but a settled predation, the hunter's patience turned against the innocent.

So the witnesses differ only in where they place the emphasis — Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott upon the shifting figure, the same man now lion and now fowler; Gill upon the spiritual quarry, the saints hunted for their faith; Henry upon the appetite behind the ambush, a cruelty that feeds with pleasure — but they do not divide over the substance. All hear in the verse the same thing: a strength that has made itself a beast of prey, and a helplessness drawn, unresisting, into the net.
10:
The hunter gathers himself for the spring, and the witnesses watch the persecutor stoop only that his victim may fall the harder: "he croucheth, and humbleth himself, that the poor may fall by his strong ones." The reformed John Gill draws out the treachery of the crouch. As the lion couches before he leaps and the fowler creeps low to draw the bird into his net, so the antichristian beast, though he has the mouth of a lion and speaks like a dragon, would be thought a lamb, meek and lowly, styling himself "servus servorum," the servant of servants — and all his humbling is but the posture of the pounce.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the same lion in view, lying close upon the ground that he may not be discovered and may the more suddenly seize his prey; and Adam Clarke, hearing in the verse the scoffing and insidious conduct of such men as Sanballat and Tobiah, notes how the lion "squats down and gathers himself together, that he may make the greater spring" (Neh. 4).

The grammatical-historical witnesses find a real crux in the words. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the Chethib against the Keri and take Job's lioness couching in her den as the rule of interpretation (Job 38:40), noting that the verb for "crouch down" is otherwise unsupported in Hebrew but answered by kindred Arabic words for making even, for creeping stealthily, and for a hunter's hiding-place. Charles Ellicott records the sharper difference: while the received text has the wicked crouch, some — Jerome and the Syriac among them — render "is crushed," making the sufferer the subject, so that it is the poor man who is beaten down and sinks; and the puzzling "by his strong ones" he would read either of the lion's strong claws, keeping the figure, or, on the darkness-root he has urged before, of the persecutor lying "darkly down in his strong places."

Here, then, the witnesses genuinely divide over who stoops and who falls: whether the wicked crouches like a beast to spring, as Gill, Wesley, and Keil and Delitzsch have it, or the afflicted is crushed and sinks beneath his mighty ones, as Jerome and the Syriac would read. Yet the drift of the verse survives either rendering, for on both there is a strong one gathering himself and a weak one going down; and the crouch that looks like humility is, all agree, the most dangerous posture the persecutor takes.
11:
"He hath said in his heart, God hath forgotten" — the persecutor's cruelty is traced at last to its root, a practical atheism, and the witnesses hear in it the creed that makes all the rest possible. The reformed John Gill weighs what it is that God is thought to have forgotten: either the wicked man's own sins, not being immediately punished, so that he presumes upon a lasting impunity, though God will yet remember the iniquities of Babylon and render double; or else the poor ones he oppresses, who seem for a while forgotten, though a book of remembrance is written for them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the settled despair of the enemy who says God "hath cast off this people, and will never more re-establish them," and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens only the tense, "he hideth his face" being better "hath hidden."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as a threefold blasphemy. When his own conscience asks how he will answer to the Judge of heaven and earth, the persecutor turns it off with "God hath forgotten, he hideth his face, he will never see it," which is a reproach cast at once upon God's omniscience and providence, as if he could not see; upon his holiness, as if, seeing, he did not hate; and upon his justice, as if, hating, he would never call the wicked to account. Those who suffer from such oppressors, Henry adds, may take comfort that men abusive to God's people are abusive to God Almighty himself, and he will in due time appear for them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark that with this boast, "God hath forgotten," the description of the ungodly reaches its lowest point, and that it is precisely here — where the six letterless strophes end — that the acrostic gathers itself to resume: over against the man who says God has forgotten, the psalmist will cry in the next breath that God should not forget, taking up the very word and turning it into prayer.

So the witnesses do not divide. Whether the thing forgotten be the sinner's own guilt or the sufferer's cause, and whether the atheism be read as presumption or as despair, all agree that the persecutor's whole strength rests upon a lie about God — that he neither sees nor remembers — and that the psalm has led the reader down to this false creed only in order to answer it.
12:
Against the lie that God has forgotten, the psalm flings its great counter-cry, and the witnesses feel the whole movement turn here from complaint to petition: "Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up thine hand." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the structural moment — "here the acrostic arrangement is resumed with koph" — for in contrast to those who have no God, or only a lifeless idol, the psalmist calls upon the living God to destroy the very appearance of his indifference by arising to act, lifting up his hand at once to help and to punish, and "forget not the humble" being, in their reading, a prayer that God fulfil his own remembered nature against the "God hath forgotten" of the ungodly (Ps. 9:12).

The puritan-evangelical witnesses hear the boldness and the tenderness of the prayer together. Matthew Henry has David beg that God would himself appear — "Arise, O Lord, to the confusion of those who say that thou hidest thy face" — and then appear for his people, "forget not the humble, the afflicted, the poor, the poor in spirit," whose oppressors say God has forgotten them and who, in their own despair, are half ready to say the same. Charles Spurgeon marvels at the mingling of confidence and unbelief in the words: "with what bold language will faith address its God, and yet what unbelief is mingled with our strongest confidence," for fearlessly the Lord is stirred up to arise, yet timidly begged not to forget the humble, as if Jehovah could ever be forgetful of his saints. This verse, Spurgeon says, is the incessant cry of the Church until her Lord shall come.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the petition as a summons to both mercy and judgment: "hear their reproaches, see their guile, consider thy oppressed people; lift up thine hand, threaten them, that they may desist and repent," and, if they will not repent, that they be punished.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the verse is the hinge of the psalm, the point at which the long, grieved description of the wicked breaks off and the sufferer turns his face wholly to God; and they hear in "lift up thine hand" and "forget not the humble" the two things faith always asks in such an hour — that God would show his power, and that in showing it he would remember the least of those who wait for him.
13:
The prayer that God would arise carries in its heart a question flung at the wicked, and the witnesses hear the psalmist marvel that such contempt should ever be spoken: "wherefore doth the wicked contemn God?" The reformed John Gill lists the ways God is despised — when his being and providence are denied, his word derided and the great things of his law counted a strange thing, his gospel reckoned foolishness, and his ministers and above all his Son treated with disdain — all of which, in his reading, the man of sin has done. The wesleyan-arminian voices press the mystery of God's forbearance: Adam Clarke asks how the Lord permits such persons to triumph, and answers that "the longsuffering of God leadeth them to repentance"; John Wesley turns the question toward that very patience, "why dost thou, by giving them impunity, suffer and occasion them to despise thee?"

The puritan-evangelical witnesses feel the double astonishment of the verse. Matthew Henry hears the psalmist wonder both at the wickedness and at the patience — why do the wicked speak so impiously, so absurdly, casting contempt on the holy God? because they do not know him; and why are they suffered to do so? because the day of reckoning is not yet come, and the measure of their iniquity is not yet full. Charles Spurgeon traces the whole evil of the persecutor to this source, "atheistical ideas with regard to the government of the world," for he despises the Lord because he will not believe that sin will meet with punishment, having "said in his heart, Thou wilt not require it"; and Spurgeon adds the grim rejoinder that "if there were no hell for other men, there ought to be one for those who question the justice of it."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch already look past the taunt to its answer, reading the verse as the last height of the wicked man's presumption before the psalmist confronts it: the ungodly imagines God will not require it, but it is with God entirely otherwise than he supposes, for — as the next verse will insist — he does see.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the contempt of God is the spring of the persecutor's whole conduct, that its very speech is "Thou wilt not require it," and that the outrageousness of the thought is itself a plea, for a God so despised has every reason, in his own cause, to arise.
14:
To the wicked man's "thou wilt not require it" the psalm returns a flat contradiction, and the witnesses gather on the certainty that answers his atheism: "thou hast seen it." The reformed John Gill sets the confession squarely against the boast — though the wicked say God will never see, he sees all things and all men, every action, and every thing in particular, even what is said or thought in the heart. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the line as the deliberate answer to v.11: it is with God wholly otherwise than the ungodly imagine, for he does behold the mischief and the spite, noting it all "to give it into his hand," which is to take it into his own power and keeping. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke joins the seeing to the requiting — "nothing can escape thy notice; thou hast not forgotten thy justice, though judgment be not speedily executed" — and hears in the sufferer's committing of himself the surrender of body, soul, and cause to the God who will not forget him; John Wesley glosses the requital "with thy hand" as God's own extraordinary providence, put forth just because the oppressed were destitute of all other help.

The puritan-evangelical witnesses turn the divine oversight into comfort. Matthew Henry bids the persecuted encourage themselves not only that God has seen the mischief but that he beholds it still, all that is done by the hands and all the spite that lurks in the hearts of oppressors, and will yet recompense it into their bosoms; and he reads "the poor committeth himself unto thee" of a people who rely on God as their patron and refer their cause to him as their Judge. Charles Spurgeon puts it most memorably — "God is all-eye to see, and all-hand to punish his enemies" — so that from divine oversight there is no hiding and from divine justice no fleeing.

The one dissent is textual, and it is Charles Ellicott's. He would render the opening of the sufferer's clause not "the poor committeth himself unto thee" but "the helpless leaveth it to Thee"; and, by a slight change in the division and pointing of the letters, he floats a bolder reading still, "it is against thee that he is strong in darkness," carrying over the darkness-root he has found in the peculiar word for the poor. The rest do not follow him; but whether the helpless man commits himself or leaves his cause with God, the witnesses agree on the heart of the verse, that the eye which the wicked thought was shut has seen everything, and the hand he thought was slack is the hand into which all his mischief is being gathered.
15:
Having pleaded that God sees, the psalm now asks that he strike, and the witnesses take up the double petition: "break thou the arm of the wicked and the evil man; seek out his wickedness till thou find none." On the first clause they agree — the "arm" is the persecutor's power, and to break it is to leave him unable to hold the sword or do the mischief he did; the reformed John Gill hears the prayer already in part fulfilled upon antichrist, whose arm is broken though his kingdom is not yet dashed to pieces, and notes that the accent divides the verse, so that "and the evil man" belongs rather with what follows.

It is the second clause that divides the witnesses, for "seek out his wickedness till thou find none" may be read two ways. The grammatical-historical voices take it as a proverb of utter riddance. Keil and Delitzsch insist that "to seek and not find," said of that which has wholly disappeared, is the language here: "mayst thou punish his wickedness, mayst thou find nothing more of it," so that what is no longer visible even to the eye of God has absolutely vanished out of existence, an absolute conquest of evil as sure as God's own everlasting kingship. Charles Ellicott reads the same proverb, citing the like phrase where seeking and not finding expresses the riddance of evil (Isa. 41:12), and renders, "thou shalt look for his wickedness and not find it," the Septuagint agreeing, "his sin shall be sought, and shall not be found."

The wesleyan-arminian and puritan-evangelical witnesses hear rather a searching-out for punishment. Adam Clarke has God investigate all the persecutor's public haunts and private ways, bringing every villainy to light and continuing to punish "while there is a crime to punish," or "till not one transgressor is to be found"; John Wesley reads it plainly, "search for it, and punish these wicked atheists, till no such wickedness be left." Matthew Henry sets the whole in his exposition of the prayer against the persecutors, that God would both disable them — "break the arm of the wicked, that the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared" (Job 34:30) — and deal with them, seeking out the wickedness they thought should for ever lie hid and unpunished.

So the debate is real: whether the line prays that God so hunt out the sinner's evil as to make it disappear altogether from the world, or that he search it out in order to bring every hidden crime to punishment. Under either reading the witnesses agree on the end sought, a world, or at least a church, in which the wickedness of the wicked is at last not to be found.
16:
"The LORD is King for ever and ever" — the psalm lifts of a sudden from petition to triumph, and the witnesses hear in the acclamation the ground of every hope that has gone before. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the widening: if the psalm has hitherto been personal, "it here swells out into a larger strain of national hope and faith." Keil and Delitzsch place the poet on an eminence from which he seems to behold the end, basking in what has been obtained by prayer, for the ardent longing of the meek for the arising of Jahve has now been heard (Isa. 26:8).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry grounds the confidence in the office of a King: it belongs to a king to administer justice, and to whom should injured subjects appeal but to the sovereign — "Help, my Lord, O King!" — while this King, unlike any earthly prince, is everlasting, and can by an eternal judgment dispense rewards and punishments in a state where time shall be no more. Charles Spurgeon reads the verse as the psalm's closing song of thanksgiving to the great and everlasting King, who has granted the desire of his humble people and punished the heathen that trampled upon his poor.

Over the second clause, "the heathen are perished out of his land," the witnesses read at different depths. The wesleyan-arminian voices take it historically: John Wesley of the Canaanites whom God, as King of the world, expelled from the land he calls his own, confirming thereby the faith of his people for the future; Adam Clarke of the same nations, all "either cut off or converted." The reformed John Gill reaches forward to the last things, when Christ shall be King over all the earth, every antichristian power destroyed and the devil, beast, and false prophet cast into the lake of fire, and his kingdom an everlasting one that no usurper shall obtain.

So the witnesses differ in their reach — some looking back to the Canaanites rooted out of Canaan, some forward to every enemy perished from the kingdom of Christ — but they do not divide over the truth that carries the verse. The King is eternal, and because his throne does not pass, the case of his oppressed people is never desperate; the heathen perish out of his land, but the Lord remains, King for ever and ever.
17:
The song of the eternal King turns at once to the prayer he has heard, and the witnesses dwell on the tender order of grace the verse discloses: "LORD, thou hast heard the desire of the humble." The reformed John Gill observes that the prayers here owned are not always spoken aloud, for "the prayers of God's people sometimes lie in inward and secret desires of the soul, and are not expressed in words"; yet these heart-desires are all before the Lord and principally regarded by him, being his own preparation and the breathings of his Spirit, and the desires of humble souls he never despises nor sends away empty.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the whole economy of that grace in four steps: God prepares the heart, suggests the prayer, hears what is prayed, and answers the petition; so that "he who has got a cry in his heart after God may rest assured that that cry proceeded from a divine preparation," and that an answer will surely come, for no man ever had such a cry but from God. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the sense of "thou wilt prepare their heart," reading it of God's giving and preserving in his people the right disposition toward himself, what the New Testament calls the single eye, the fixed and steadfast heart that is turned wholly to him (Ps. 51:12).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a little doctrine of answered prayer. God, he says, never said to a distressed suppliant, "Seek in vain"; and he keeps a settled method, first preparing the heart of his people and then giving the answer of peace, so that "God's working upon us is the best earnest of his working for us." He prepares the heart by kindling holy desires, strengthening faith, fixing the thoughts and raising the affections, and then graciously accepts the prayer he himself has wrought; and since "the preparation of the heart is from the Lord," we must seek to him even for that (Prov. 16:1).

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the humble are heard, that their very desires are God's own planting, and that the same grace which disposes the heart to pray is the pledge that the prayer will not return empty — so that the verse binds together, in one movement, the preparing of the suppliant and the hearing of his suit.
18:
The psalm ends where the sufferer's whole hope has been tending, in the judgment that sets the helpless free and silences the tyrant: God will hear "to judge the fatherless and the oppressed, that the man of the earth may no more oppress." The reformed John Gill reads it of God's causing his ear to hear the cries of his people so as to avenge the wrongs done to the fatherless and the oppressed by the man of sin. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the two things God will do: he will plead the cause of the persecuted, judging the fatherless and oppressed and clearing their innocency, and he will put an end to the fury of the persecutors — "hitherto shall they come, but no further." And Henry now makes light of the very oppressor he had so darkly drawn, for the man is "but a man of the earth, a man out of the earth," sprung from it and hastening back to it, mean and weak and mortal (Isa. 51:12): why fear the fury of one whom God holds in a chain and can restrain at will, when he that protects us is the Lord of heaven?

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the deliverance home. John Wesley reads "to judge" as to give sentence for the oppressed and against their enemies, and "the man" of earthly, mortal men who yet presume to contend with their Maker. Adam Clarke would render the close, "that he may not add any more to drive away the wretched man from the land," and turns it upon the persecutions of his own day, when many for their religion were driven from farm and house and employment by "the vile man of the earth," in whose sight piety toward God is the highest of crimes.

The one difference is Charles Ellicott's, and it is one of rendering. The grammatical-historical voice takes "the man of the earth" not of the oppressor but of mere mortal man over against God: the clause means "that man of the earth may no more terrify," or, comparing the like word in the ninth psalm (Ps. 9:20), "that the nations of the earth may know themselves to be but men," and no longer defy Israel and Israel's God.

So the witnesses part only over whom the last word humbles — the single tyrant driven from the land, or all the proud nations taught that they are but men — yet they close in one accord. The God who was thought to stand afar off has arisen to judge; the fatherless is righted, and the man of the earth, whether tyrant or heathen, is put in his place at last, that he may oppress no more.
